blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define a conflict between macroeconomic aims, trace how it arises, and keep a possible cause apart from its consequence.

blocks.heading: What a conflict of aims is
blocks.text: A conflict between macroeconomic aims is a situation in which the conditions that serve one aim make another harder to achieve, so pushing towards one destination means moving away from another at the same time. The clearest case runs through how much the whole economy spends. When spending rises quickly across the economy, firms take on more workers and unemployment tends to fall, which serves the jobs aim. Where workplaces are near full, the same pressure tends to push prices up, straining the inflation aim, and part of the extra spending goes abroad on imports, widening a current account deficit. Chasing the growth aim hard in these conditions tends to pull the other aims out of reach.

blocks.heading: A conflict in numbers
blocks.text: One year spending across an economy grows fast. Its unemployment rate falls from 16.0% to 13.5%, which moves it towards the jobs aim. Its inflation rate rises from 3.8% to 6.9%, which moves it away from the inflation aim. Spending on imports grows by 9.0% while export earnings grow by 4.0%, so the current account moves towards a bigger deficit. Brazil's boom years showed the same shape: quick growth and low unemployment at first, then faster price rises and strain on the country's external accounts. The government reading these faces a ranking decision: easing the pressure on prices would mean cooling the spending that created the jobs.

blocks.heading: The three conflicts to know
blocks.text: Three conflicts between aims stand out. Full employment versus stable prices: as unemployment falls, firms compete for the workers who remain, so wages tend to rise faster, and where output cannot keep up with the extra spending from those wages, prices tend to rise too. Economic growth versus balance of payments stability: as output and incomes grow, households and firms buy more of everything, including imports - for Namibia, vehicles, fuel and machinery come largely from abroad - so where export earnings do not rise as fast, the current account deficit widens. Full employment versus balance of payments stability: more people in work means more income spent, and part of it goes on imports; and where a tight labour market pushes wages up faster than in trading partners, the country's exports tend to become dearer abroad, so export earnings may grow more slowly. In each pair the link is the same - more spending across the economy - working on two aims in opposite directions. Whether a conflict appears depends on conditions: where there is spare capacity and many people out of work, spending can rise without much pressure on prices, and where the extra output is sold abroad, growth can strengthen the current account rather than weaken it.

blocks.heading: Cause or consequence?
blocks.text: A common error is labelling a possible cause as a consequence, or the reverse, when writing about conflicts between aims. The boundary runs along the direction of the arrow: a quick rise in spending across the economy can be a cause of faster rises in prices; faster rises in prices are the consequence of it. The test is to ask whether the named item sets the change in motion or follows from it. If a figure or event starts the process, it is a cause; if it results from the process, it is a consequence. A learner who writes that price rises cause spending to grow has reversed a relationship that runs the other way in this analysis.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Aims can move together where growth comes from rising productivity rather than spending pressure; the tools a government uses to steer between its aims are examined in topic 4.3, and the aims connect forward to growth in topic 4.6 and jobs in topic 4.7.
